newsitem.title: USA: Consumers seek Internet access to USDA salmonella reports.
newsitem.headline: Consumers seek Internet access to USDA salmonella reports.

text.p: A plan to make Agriculture Department safety reports available to consumers on the Internet has ruffled the feathers of the poultry industry, which claims the move would put them at a competitive disadvantage.

This summer, the agency will begin testing raw meat and poultry at slaughter plants for salmonella as part of a major overhaul of U.S. meat inspection announced by the Clinton administration last year. Salmonella is the biggest food-borne killer.
By law, the information must be available to the public and the Agriculture Department said it was considering releasing the reports on the Internet.

Poultry and meat producers at a Thursday hearing objected to the Internet access, saying consumers will not know how to interpret the test results from slaughter plants. They also claimed the information would be used by foreign competitors to block U.S. exports or as a means to negotiate prices.
"We feel the department should give very serious consideration to not posting this information on the Internet," Ken May of the National Broiler Council told the meeting.
Consumer groups said access to the poultry and meat inspections was no different than being able to see U.S. airline safety records.

"The taxpayers are paying for the government to collect the information and we want the information," said Caroline Smith DeWaal of the Centre for Science in the Public Interest. "It's a huge revolution in how the industry is evaluated."
The Agriculture Department must also decide exactly what kinds of information to make available online.

Consumer groups want to know the name of the plant, the location, the product line tested and how the results compared with government standards. But the industry contends that individual plants should not be reported until they fail to meet government standards three times and are deemed to be in violation of the rules.
Thomas Billy, head of the Agriculture Department's Food Safety Inspection Service, said it could take several months for the agency to decide whether it will publish the information online.
